# Learning Modes And Embeddings

Transaction histories can inform several business decisions, from payment
review to account retention. A learned history vector can be tested as a
common input to separate predictors for these tasks, alongside existing
spending summaries. This lets you evaluate reuse of the context learned from
your records. Each predictor still needs its own task labels and held-out
assessment.

An embedding is a numeric representation of the context the model has learned.
Set `embed=True` where you want to export one. The model still needs a learning
objective, such as a supervised dispute target.

## Choose Where To Export

This model learns to predict payment disputes and exports the payment context
and a summary of the account's recent transactions:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    embed=True,
    amount=rf.Number,
    merchant=rf.Category,
    recent_transactions=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        embed=True,
        amount=rf.Number,
        merchant=rf.Category,
        days_ago=rf.Number,
    ),
    disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
)
```

| `embed=True` location | Exported representation |
| --- | --- |
| Root | The root's reduced context. |
| Branch | The branch's reduced context. |
| Leaf | The decoder's pooled context before its datatype output head. |

The `xs` preset uses one-output reductions. This example therefore exports one
payment vector and one history-summary vector per payment. It does not export
one vector per transaction. A nested branch inside the history would retain
those outer transaction positions when exporting its own summary.

A leaf embedding is different from its raw input embedding: it can include
ancestor context and visible, aligned sibling fields. A branch embedding
summarizes the inputs controlled by that branch's reduction.

## Read The Output

After [training](../guides/lightning.qmd), read prediction inputs from your
application's Parquet file:

```python
import pyarrow.compute as pc

requests = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    model=model,
    predict="payments/requests.parquet",
)
predictions = model.predict(
    datamodule=requests, batch_size=256, devices=1,
)["predictions"]
payment_embedding = pc.struct_field(
    pc.struct_field(predictions, "/"),
    "embedding",
)
history_embedding = pc.struct_field(
    pc.struct_field(predictions, "/recent_transactions"),
    "embedding",
)
```

Exported vectors are float32 and L2-normalized along their `d_model` axis;
zero vectors remain zero. Repeated outer coordinates use fixed-size Arrow
lists for finite branch limits and variable-size lists for `length=None`.
Multiple learned reduction outputs retain a fixed-size list axis. See
[Prediction Output](../guides/prediction-output.qmd) for the full Arrow contract.

`rf.Attention(n_outputs=...)` exports multiple reduction outputs.
`reduction=None` retains routed child slots, whose count depends on branch
length and child outputs. These choices change the shape of the representation;
see [Branch](../data-types/branch.qmd).

Evaluate an embedding on its intended downstream task. A useful dispute
predictor does not by itself establish useful similarity or clustering.
Preserve the schema and trained state with
[the model artifact](../guides/lightning.qmd#save-and-load).

To evaluate a frozen representation, keep the exporting model fixed and
generate vectors in prediction mode for the training and held-out
observations. Fit separate task predictors using only the training vectors
and labels. Keep the exporting model fixed throughout: this measures what a
downstream predictor can learn from the representation as exported.

Choose cohort and time boundaries before training. For an evaluation on
unseen accounts, exclude held-out accounts from both representation learning
and downstream predictor training. Each history vector represents the account
at a defined decision cutoff; the task label records an outcome over a later
period. Keep records after that cutoff out of the input snapshot.

Compare existing features alone, vectors alone, and their combination on the
same observations. Choose predictor settings on the same validation split and
assess the fixed choices on test data. For account-closure prediction,
evaluate precision and recall at a fixed contact capacity. For payment review,
measure dispute recall at a fixed review capacity. These task metrics help
decide whether the reusable representation earns a place in the workflow.
[Learning From Event Histories](../guides/learning-from-event-data.qmd) explains
how to prepare the observations and outcome windows for these experiments.

## Learn Without A Label

A model can also learn by reconstructing values hidden from otherwise
unlabeled records. For example, replace the supervised target with sampled
reconstruction of transaction amounts and merchant categories:

```python
model = rf.Model.xs(
    embed=True,
    recent_transactions=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        days_ago=rf.Number,
        amount=rf.Number(mask=rf.Mask(rate=0.15, reconstruct=True)),
        merchant=rf.Category(mask=rf.Mask(rate=0.10, reconstruct=True)),
    ),
)
```

`embed=True` alone creates no objective. Sampled reconstruction supplies the
learning signal in this example; it does not request ordinary decoded
prediction output. [Masking](dynamic-masking.qmd) explains that distinction.
Supervised and sampled reconstruction objectives can coexist, with each leaf's
`weight` scaling its contribution.

[Pretraining And Fine-Tuning](../guides/pretraining.qmd) shows how to transfer
reconstruction training to a labeled task. The
[reconstruction transfer proof](../proofs/representation/reconstruction-transfer.html)
compares frozen root embeddings with raw features, an untrained encoder, and
training on independently permuted views.
